League of Legends · Ranked Solo · North America · Pre-Season 2016

League of Legends:
The map of
champion matchups

Illustrative lineup, not a real match: Garen, Lee Sin, Ahri, Jinx, Thresh vs Darius, Vi, Yasuo, Caitlyn, Leona.

Does Ahri beat Yasuo? Does anyone really counter anyone? We took every pair of champions that met on opposite teams in 222,616 ranked games, and asked which matchups are real, which are noise, and which are just one champion being strong.

Key findings

There is a map, but it is mostly a map of strength. Champions differ in how often they win, and that shows up in nearly every clear matchup. Pair-specific counters, if any, are faint: no single pair clears the bar, and we find no rock-paper-scissors loops, in this dataset.

  • Strong champions beat weak ones, and it carries over to later games: 600 of 606 clear edges point from the stronger to the weaker champion, and 87% keep their direction in held-out games.
  • Beyond strength, the pair-level signal is tiny: interactions explain about 1.2% of the variance in pair win rates, and 1 of 7,324 testable pairs pass the filter.
  • Rock-paper-scissors loops: 0 among 540 triangles of clear edges. Fake worlds with no counters at all give about the same.

01Reading a matchup

One win rate is a small sample.

A matchup win rate is just a count: of the games in which champion A met champion B, A’s team won some share. With 128 champions there are 8,128 pairs and 222,616 matches, which sounds like a lot. But the typical pair meets only about 210 times in the games we use for discovery, so most cells are thin. Three habits keep thin cells from fooling us: show an uncertainty interval, shrink small samples toward 50%, and judge every claim only on games we held back.

02The map

The 128 × 128 map

Each cell is one matchup: the row champion against the column champion, showing how often the row champion’s team wins. Blue means the row champion wins more, orange means it wins less, and faint cells have few games. “Opposite teams” counts every cross-team meeting (25 per match). “Same lane” counts only true lane matchups, where each team has exactly one player in the same position. Switch to “beyond strength”, which subtracts each champion’s overall strength, and watch most of the map go quiet.

03The network

The network of advantages

Draw an arrow from champion A to champion B when A beats B clearly enough to survive a false-discovery filter. Drawing every arrow makes a hairball, so each champion keeps only its few strongest arrows by default. Arrange the champions by strength and the picture is telling: arrows run downhill, strong champions beat weak ones, and almost nothing runs uphill or in a circle.

04Strength

Strength or counter?

A champion that wins 53% of its games will beat almost everyone, so a raw matchup table is mostly a list of strong champions. To separate the two, we fit one strength number per champion (a Bradley–Terry-style logistic model, the same “main effects” model as the T3 test in the first essay) and ask what is left over for each pair.

05Is it real?

Is it real? Test it on games the analysis never saw.

A pattern found in the discovery games should show up again in later games. We split by game build: discovery on the earlier builds (112,921 matches), checking on the later ones (93,460). If a matchup edge is real, a pair that looked good for A in discovery should still look good for A in the check.

06Noise check

How much of this is noise?

We re-ran the whole pipeline on fake worlds. In a shuffled world, game outcomes are scrambled among games of the same build, so no champion matters at all. In a strength-only world, outcomes are simulated from the fitted strengths and nothing else: champions differ in strength, but no pair has a special matchup. Every fake world gets the same tests and the same false-discovery filter as the real data. We made 200 worlds of each kind.

What this says. Shuffled worlds produce 0.0 significant edges on average (never more than 1), so the filter does what it promises. Strength-only worlds produce 592 edges (95% range 511–669); the real data has 606. Beyond strength, strength-only worlds produce 0.0 edges on average and the real data has 1. Without the filter, 378 pairs reach p < 0.05 beyond strength where 269–334 would be expected by chance: a small excess that no single pair can be separated from. The real data has 0 loops among 540 triangles of significant edges, and strength-only worlds also have about 0. With no filter at all, 10.9% of triangles look like rock-paper-scissors in the real data, against 10.3% in strength-only worlds and 23.4% in shuffled ones. The real data is about as ordered as strength-only worlds and far more ordered than shuffled ones, so the loops that remain look like leftover noise, not designed counters.

07Verdict

So: is there a map of counters?

There is a map, but it is mostly a map of strength. Champions differ in how often they win, and that shows up in nearly every clear matchup. Pair-specific counters, if any, are faint: no single pair clears the bar, and we find no rock-paper-scissors loops, in this dataset.

What the data supports

  • Strong champions beat weak ones, and it carries over to later games: 600 of 606 clear edges point from the stronger to the weaker champion, and 87% keep their direction in held-out games.
  • Beyond strength, the pair-level signal is tiny: interactions explain about 1.2% of the variance in pair win rates, and 1 of 7,324 testable pairs pass the filter.
  • Rock-paper-scissors loops: 0 among 540 triangles of clear edges. Fake worlds with no counters at all give about the same.
  • Same-lane matchups carry more specific signal than all-pairs ones, but only 87% of the clear lane edges keep their direction in held-out games, and the pattern follows strength.

What it does not tell us

  • It cannot rule counters out. A real counter worth one or two points would be invisible with a few hundred games per pair. Our test is predictive, as in the first essay’s T3 test.
  • It is not causal. Players choose champions into matchups they expect to win, game builds differ, teammates differ, and positions are detected by a heuristic.
  • It is not today’s game: one 2016 pre-season, one region, ranked solo queue.
  • Most pairs have too few games to say anything: only 7,324 of 8,128 pairs have 50+ discovery games, and the typical pair has 210.

Status: exploratory results from the 2026-07-21 data rerun, not peer reviewed. Robustness checks and an independent review are still pending.

Methods and provenance

Data

LoLA-2016: 222,616 ranked solo (5×5) matches of at least 10 minutes from the North America server, Pre-Season 2016, from the cleaned Parquet v2 export (HMAC-pseudonymised). Every pair of champions on opposite teams is one view of a match, so each match gives 25 views. Only aggregated counts are used on this page.

Methods

Cohort, splits and positions follow the benchmark code. Discovery uses the earlier builds (112,921 matches); the later builds (93,460) are used only to check claims; the validation set picks the regularisation for the strength model (candidates 0.01, 0.1 and 1; the least-shrunk value 1 was used for the adjustment, and validation log-loss differs by at most 0.0003 between them). Pair significance: normal-approximation binomial test against 50% for pairs with at least 50 games, Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery control over those pairs. Strength is centred within role (every team has exactly one player per role, so role-level offsets cannot be told apart from the data), so it reads as better or worse than a typical champion in the same role. Beyond strength: observed minus expected wins from the strength model, standardised by the binomial variance. Shrinkage: empirical-Bayes beta-binomial. Same lane: players whose position is determined from the 0–10 minute lane and role, and only matches with exactly one such player per team. Fake worlds: 200 shuffles within build and 200 simulations from the fitted strengths, each refitted and re-tested; random seed 20260721.

Limitations

Predictive and descriptive, not causal. One season, one region, ranked solo queue. Match number is only a proxy for time, and the build split is a description of drift, not a test of it. Champion picks are selected: players pick into matchups they expect to win. Position detection is heuristic (96.4% of players mapped; same-lane coverage 86–98% by position). Pair views within a match are not independent of each other; we check false discoveries against fake worlds rather than assuming the test is perfect. Thin pairs are shrunk but still uncertain. Champion names are English.
